flagged.evidence: The definition permits an empty finite family H but says “h is chosen uniformly from H.” For U={0,1}, R={0}, and H=emptyset, all stated finiteness and function-family conditions hold, but no uniform random h exists. Thus the displayed probability and hence the definition are undefined without H nonempty.

The Remark says “Pairwise independence forces each individual value h(x) to be uniform on R.” Under the stated definition this fails when U has one element: let U={x}, R={0,1}, and H={h} with h(x)=0. The condition over two distinct inputs is vacuous, so H is pairwise independent by this definition, while h(x) is not uniform.

Step 1.1 begins “Fix any deterministic language A” and computes its answer D(x). The cited PP definition requires a probabilistic polynomial-time machine, but an arbitrary decidable deterministic language need not have a polynomial-time decider, so this construction need not be a PP machine. It needs A in P (or an explicitly fixed easy language) to witness the claimed PP counterexample.

The Statement bounds the “total number of configurations of M on those inputs” for all inputs of a fixed length n. Take a fixed one-tape machine that reads its first cell and immediately accepts, with s(n)=1. Every branch visits one cell, but its initial configurations over x in {0,1}^n are 2^n distinct because the tape convention defines the initial tape t_x using all symbols of x. This contradicts a bound 2^{c_M} for fixed c_M. Step 1.1 counts only visited portions and thereby omits these differing unvisited input contents.

The item quantifies only over an abstract field F and matrices A,B,C in M_n(F), yet calls the test “randomized polynomial time.” The probabilistic-machine definition requires input strings and a polynomial in their length. No encoding of F-elements or matrices, nor effective polynomial-time field operations, is assumed. The proof establishes an algebraic operation bound, not a probabilistic Turing-machine bound over an arbitrary field.

The Statement assumes merely that “S subseteq F [is] finite,” then chooses uniformly from S^n and writes d/|S|. For S=emptyset, the uniform choice is undefined (for n>=1) and the denominator is zero. A nonempty-sample-set hypothesis is required.

The Statement does not restrict n to be positive; the cited multivariate-polynomial definition explicitly sets R[x_1,...,x_0]:=R. But the proof starts its induction at “For n=1” and supplies no n=0 case, so it does not establish the stated zero-variable instance (a nonzero constant polynomial).
